title.narrative: Promoting Resource Efficiency and Circularity to Reduce Plastic Pollution for Asia and the Pacific

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

This project will deliver socio-economic benefits for diverse communities by reducing marine plastic pollution and restoring the health of rivers, coasts and marine ecosystems. Nearly 700,000 metric tons of plastic litter will be avoided because of this project. Ocean plastics have direct economic implications for poor communities and especially women who rely on marine life and ecosystems for their livelihoods.[i] The economic costs of plastic are also felt by people who rely on agriculture as waste often chokes rice fields and other crops.[ii] The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant setbacks in waste management and efforts to transition to a circular plastics economy. In addition to the increased volumes of medical waste and single-use plastics, the COVID-19 pandemic also resulted in loss of livelihoods in the waste management industry. In May 2020, an estimated 63,000 waste workers reportedly lost their livelihood in Indonesia alone.[iii] A green and blue recovery from COVID-19 that incorporates waste management, a circular plastics economy, and livelihood creation is crucial. Decent work – jobs that are fair, equitable, safe and dignified, is a core component of green and blue recovery and be trialled in the Material Recovery Facilities, adjacent to the pilot communities. Investing in infrastructure, waste management systems, and communities ensures a resilient future for the economy and environment. This will be demonstrated at a local scale in two communities: Tan An (VIE) and Cirebon (INDO) which have been selected for pilot demonstration projects. The direct beneficiaries of the project include 1000 members (50% women) who will be included in activities to understand their attitudes and practices in relation to plastic and be encouraged to adopt behaviors to eliminate, innovate and circulate plastic. Supported by activities in Plastik Sulit, the project will offer women workshops and activities to build their capacity in circular economy solutions, design-thinking, business/financial planning and other skills to nurture circular innovations and SMEs.Community pilot activities and other project activities, including new packaging solutions and better governance for plastic waste management and a circular economy, will provide critical public health benefits by providing alternatives to the dumping or burning of plastic. Circular solutions will decrease negative toxin releases from burning plastics, including exposure to furans and dioxins (unintentional POPs) and other negative health outcomes recognized by the Basel and Stockholm Conventions (as outlined in section 7). Plastic toxicity interacts with female bodies differently to male and especially impacts women’s reproductive health, their breastmilk, pregnancies and unborn children.[iv][v] Women, men and children in the pilot communities will benefit from decreases in the volume of plastic waste accumulating around community dwellings and blocking waterways and sewers. Reducing plastic pollution can contribute to decreasing stagnant water and flooding, which is a breeding ground for disease vectors and the spread of diseases like cholera. In this respect the project contributes to global health equity and especially for women since the burden of plastic falls more heavily on the poor and on women. Across the partner DMCs, gender roles structure the social expectations that women will provide water and care for the ill, the infirm, the elderly and babies and children. The project will also contribute to:· Restored and sustained freshwater, coastal, and marine ecosystems, including globally significant biodiversity;· Reduced vulnerability to climate risks, and increased ecosystem resilience through reduced greenhouse gas emissions as a result of reduced plastics production and waste, and better integrated primary collection and sorting (e.g., reduction of volume of wastes in illegal dumpsites, diversion of waste away from landfills and improved management of plastic wastes); and· Indirectly, reduced and/or avoided chemicals of global concern and their waste in the environment and in processes, materials and products. · Economic and social empowerment of women by leveraging opportunities across the value chain for women’s employment, training, leadership and livelihood opportunities and supporting gender-responsive waste reforms and investments.
